question: A 55-year-old asthmatic patient goes to the ER with an exacerbation. One hour after the administration of supplemental oxygen and two nebulizations of salbutamol the patient does not improve. On examination, he breathed at 42 rpm with supraclavicular drainage and presented disseminated inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. The peak flow has dropped from 310 to 220 L / min. A gasometry extracted with oxygen at 28% shows a pO2 of 54 mmHg and a pCO2 of 35 mmHg. Which of the following attitudes seems LESS indicated?

options.opc: Nebulize ipratropium bromide together with salbutamol every 20 minutes.

analysis: The patient is experiencing a severe asthma exacerbation with significant respiratory distress, evidenced by high respiratory rate, wheezing, and low peak flow. The arterial blood gas shows hypoxemia (pO2 of 54 mmHg) but normal pCO2, indicating that the patient is likely hyperventilating. In this scenario, increasing oxygen flow (option opa) is not the least indicated action, as the patient is hypoxic. Administering steroids (option opb) is crucial for reducing inflammation. Nebulizing ipratropium bromide (option opc) is also indicated as it can help with bronchodilation. Administering intravenous magnesium (option opd) can be beneficial in severe cases of asthma. Starting non-invasive mechanical ventilation (option ope) may be considered if the patient shows signs of respiratory failure or fatigue, but it is not the first-line approach in this scenario. Therefore, the least indicated option is to start non-invasive mechanical ventilation, as the patient may still respond to other treatments before reaching that stage.
